items.stem: A PySpark job defines several filters and selects but nothing runs until a count() is called. Why?

options.text: Transformations are lazy and execute only when an action is triggered
options.rationale: Correct: Spark builds a plan from lazy transformations and runs it when an action like count() is called.
Lazy evaluation is expected behavior, not a crash.
count() is an action, which is exactly what triggers execution.
Laziness, not emptiness, explains why nothing ran earlier.

items.explanation: Correct: Spark builds a plan from lazy transformations and runs it when an action like count() is called.

items.stem: Joining a very large DataFrame to a small lookup table is most efficient with which technique?

options.rationale: Correct: broadcasting the small table to every executor avoids a large shuffle.
Collecting a large DataFrame to the driver risks out-of-memory failures.
A cross join produces every combination and is far more expensive.
Converting to RDDs does not improve this join.

items.explanation: Correct: broadcasting the small table to every executor avoids a large shuffle.

items.stem: Which TWO are good PySpark performance practices? (Select TWO)

options.text: Prefer built-in functions over Python UDFs where possible
options.rationale: Correct: built-in functions run in the JVM and avoid UDF serialization overhead.

options.text: Cache a DataFrame that is reused many times
options.rationale: Correct: caching avoids recomputing a reused DataFrame.

options.text: Always collect() large DataFrames to the driver
options.rationale: Collecting large data to the driver is a common cause of failures.

options.text: Create thousands of tiny output partitions
options.rationale: Too many tiny partitions create overhead and small-file problems.

items.explanation: Correct: built-in functions run in the JVM and avoid UDF serialization overhead.; Correct: caching avoids recomputing a reused DataFrame.
